# Diagnosing Throttle Lag on a 2011 Infiniti G37

A reported increase in throttle lag over a six-month period on a 2011 Infiniti G37, despite the absence of Diagnostic Trouble Codes (DTCs) and full adherence to maintenance schedules, points toward specific mechanical or electrical degradation rather than a catastrophic failure. The fact that no check engine light is illuminated indicates the Powertrain Control Module (PCM) has not detected parameters exceeding its fault thresholds, which often means the issue lies in sensor drift, vacuum leaks, or actuator calibration rather than a hard component failure.

### Vacuum Integrity and Airflow Dynamics

The most common cause of "lazy" throttle response in this era of VQ37VHR engine builds is a developing vacuum leak. Even if the system maintains enough pressure to idle smoothly, small leaks in the intake manifold gasket or brake booster hose can introduce unmetered air. When you press the pedal, the PCM commands a specific airflow based on the Throttle Position Sensor (TPS) reading. If the actual airflow is lower than commanded due to a leak upstream of the Mass Air Flow (MAF) sensor, the engine runs lean momentarily until the fuel trim compensates. This creates a perceptible delay or "shudder" before the engine catches up to the requested RPM.

To verify this, you can perform a smoke test on the intake system. If smoke enters through any point other than the throttle body or spark plug tubes, you have identified the leak. Another subtle culprit is the PCV (Positive Crankcase Ventilation) valve. On many VQ engines, the PCV valve becomes sticky or fails to vent properly under load. This creates excessive crankcase pressure that restricts vacuum at the intake manifold, mimicking a throttle lag. Replacing the PCV valve is often a low-cost preventative maintenance step that yields immediate results if the issue stems here.

### Sensor Calibration and TPS Drift

Since there are no codes, the Throttle Position Sensor (TPS) is likely still within its operational range, but it may have drifted slightly out of sync with the Pedal Position Sensor (PPS). Modern ECUs rely on a closed-loop learning process where they map pedal input to throttle plate position. Over time, if the TPS output voltage does not perfectly mirror the PPS signal due to wear or heat cycling, the PCM might hesitate before fully opening the throttle to avoid commanding an impossible position.

You can check for this discrepancy using an OBD-II scanner that provides live data stream graphs. Look for a correlation between the PPS and TPS values while varying pedal input. If there is a noticeable offset or if the TPS voltage jumps erratically even with smooth pedal movement, the TPS may need recalibration via diagnostic tools like Tech 2 or proprietary Infiniti software. In rare cases, the throttle body itself has carbon buildup on the butterfly plate that prevents immediate response to the electric motor's initial command until the motor "breaks through" the resistance. Cleaning the throttle body and performing an idle relearn procedure is a standard fix for this specific symptom.

### Electrical Connections and Ground Points

Sometimes the culprit is not the sensor or the engine, but the connection between them. Corrosion at the electrical connector on the back of the TPS or the PPS can introduce resistance, causing signal noise that the PCM interprets as hesitation. Inspect these connectors for green oxidation or loose pins. Additionally, check the ground straps near the ECU and battery. A high-resistance ground path can cause voltage drops under load, leading to erratic engine behavior even if no code is set.

If you have ruled out vacuum leaks, sensor drift, and connection issues, the next logical step is to review the adaptive fuel trim values in your scanner data. Long-term fuel trims that are consistently positive indicate a chronic lean condition, which could be due to a failing oxygen sensor or a very small vacuum leak not yet detected by static tests. Addressing these underlying efficiency losses will restore the crispness of the throttle response and prevent the lag from worsening as the adaptive tables reach their saturation limits.
